name: h200s
description: A sixth of the H200 (h200): 22 of its SMs on one of its six HBM3e stacks, modelled channel by channel (16 64-bit channels at 6.25 Gb/s per pin, 800 GB/s), and a sixth of its L2, so every per-SM ratio is the part's. The study shape for memory-bandwidth experiments.

sources.PLATFORM_MEMORY_TYPE, PLATFORM_MEMORY_NU: One HBM3e stack as it is: 16 channels of 64 bits (two 32-bit pseudo-channels each). The H200's 4.8 TB/s over 6 stacks x 1024 pins is 6.25 Gb/s per pin, so a channel is 8 B x 6.25 GT/s = 50 GB/s and the stack 800 GB/s. h200 models the same memory as 32 128-bit channel pairs at 9375 MT/s for a power-of-two interleave, a third of the part's channels and banks; a sixth of the part needs no such merge because one stack has a power-of-two channel count
sources.L2_REPL_POLICY: 2 (pseudo-LRU) instead of the default FIFO. A calibrated value: the part's policy is not published. On a real H200 two workloads on disjoint SMs do not slow each other (measured ratio 1.00); with FIFO a streaming SM evicts another SM's hot lines once per L2 fill and a compute-bound GEMM beside a decode GEMM runs at 0.83-0.98 of its solo rate, with pseudo-LRU at 1.00-1.07. Solo stream, GEMM and DXA copy runs move by at most 1.6% (stream on 11 SMs 2.7%)
sources.L2_SIZE, L2_NUM_WAYS, L2_NUM_BANKS: 50 MB / 6 = 8.74 MB as 16 banks x 128 sets x 33 ways x 128 B = 8.65 MB
sources.reference: fp32_lanes is 22 SMs x 128; dram_bandwidth_gbs is a sixth of the H200's
sources.PLATFORM_MEMORY_BANK_GROUPS: 8 groups of 4 banks per pseudo-channel: JESD238B.01 Tables 4 and 5 give 16 banks per stack ID and pseudo-channel, and the 12 Gb channel of a 24 Gb x 8-high stack has two stack IDs. Which stack the H200 carries is not confirmed (16 Gb x 12-high would have 12 groups). Measured, 22 SMs streaming with the scheduler window at 32: 382 GB/s with 4 groups, 522 with 8, 523 with 16
sources.PLATFORM_MEMORY_SCHED_WINDOW: 256 bursts per channel. With Ramulator's 32 the window of a channel fed by 1408 streams held one burst of each: 74% of the enqueue attempts were refused, a row activation served 77 B and 22 SMs streaming stopped at 382 GB/s of 800; 588 at 128, 621 at 256, 636 at 512. Little's law at 45 GB/s per channel (1.4 bursts/ns) over the ~72 ns a burst stays gives about 100. Accel-Sim's H100/H200 configurations use 128 per narrower channel
sources.PLATFORM_MEMORY_INTERLEAVE_SIZE: 1 KB, one row of a pseudo-channel, with channel and bank mixed. A calibrated value: the unit is reported from the GPU's driver, not from a document (Accel-Sim uses 256 B with a hashed channel index). Measured with the window at 256 and 8 bank groups, 22 SMs: a CUDA-shaped stream (bwstream -b32) reaches 708 GB/s with 1 KB, 706 with 256 B and 493 with the plain 64 B interleave (a real H200 reaches 90% of its peak with every SM); a decode GEMM's kernel time at 11 SMs is +2% over 1 SM with 1 KB, +6% with 256 B and +25% with the plain interleave. The DXA copy delivers 111 GB/s from one SM (H200 measured about 101) and 662 GB/s from 11
sources.NUM_DXA_CORES, DXA_MAX_INFLIGHT: 8 workers per SM, each holding up to 256 lines in flight. The derived worker count is the total core count over 8 (2 here, 1 for a single SM, 16 at 132 SMs), a formula from when the DXA was a cluster-level pool, so it is fixed here per SM. Measured on one SM, 16 KB tiles, four transfers outstanding per CTA: 3 workers 65 GB/s, 4 workers 84 (94 with four memory ports), 8 workers 101, 16 workers 111; a real H200 SM delivers about 101 (29 with one transfer outstanding, 56 with two, 101 with four). The in-flight limit with 4 workers: 8 (the default) 6.7 GB/s, 32 24, 64 45, 128 75, 256 90, 512 90: 256 is the smallest that does not bind, a 16 KB tile's 256 lines
sources.DTLB_SIZE, L2_TLB_MEGA_SIZE, FPU_QUEUE_S: Per-SM values, as measured for h200q (see its sources)
sources.FETCH_INFLIGHT, FFLAGS_ACCUM: Calibrated to a measurement on our H200 (study/results_gpu/h200_warprate_summary.txt, h200_warprate_nottaken.txt): one warp issues an independent integer or FMA instruction every 1.07-1.21 clocks, with no serialisation of FP operations, and a branch, taken or not, costs 10.8-12 clocks with no sign of prediction. A lone warp fetches up to 4 instructions ahead of decode and stops at a branch until it resolves; FP flags accumulate. With them one warp issues every 3.7-3.8 cycles (11.8 integer, 21.6 FMA before); the remaining gap to the part is on the issue side. No instruction class is faster than the part; 64-warp throughput is unchanged except FMA (2.74 to 3.00 per cycle, part 4.00). 2 in flight gives 6.3 cycles per instruction, 8 with 8 buffer slots 3.8. Not measured: logic depth
sources.BRANCH_REG: 0: a resolved branch reaches the scheduler without the extra register behind the ALU's result register, which has no function. Calibrated toward the part: a taken branch costs 10.8-12 clocks on our H200 (study/results_gpu/h200_warprate_summary.txt) and 23.9 cycles here with the register, 22.9 without (br_every1; 8.86 to 8.61 and 5.49 to 5.42 cycles per instruction with a branch every 4 and 16). rtlsim and SimX agree at 0 (warp_rate at ISSUE_WIDTH 4: 50 of 52 rows to the cycle). Not measured: logic depth, which the register is there for
sources.FETCH_REQ_BUF, FLUSH_REQ_BUF, OPC_MERGE_: 0: three pipeline registers without a function of their own are left out. A fetch pick goes from the warp scheduler straight into the fetch unit's request buffer; the icache flush is merged into the first frontend slice's fetch requests by a priority mux, so that slice is no longer a cycle further from the icache than the others; the operand collectors merge into the dispatch queues without an output register. Calibrated toward the part: a taken branch costs 10.8-12 clocks on our H200 (study/results_gpu/h200_warprate_summary.txt) and 22.9 cycles here before, 19.9 with the three (br_every1, one warp); a dependent integer chain 14.49 to 13.48 cycles per instruction (part 4.84). No measured class runs faster than the part because of them: with 64 warps br_every1 is 1.23 instructions per cycle before and after (part 1.16, an overshoot that was already there) and int_ind8 1.30 (part 3.58). rtlsim and SimX agree with each at 0 at small shapes (warp_rate, 8 warps x 8 threads, issue width 4: 49 to 51 of 52 rows to the cycle, worst 0.09%); OPC_MERGE_BUF is not exercised on rtlsim with 4 collectors. Not measured: logic depth
sources.LANE_DISPATCH_GAPLESS: 1 (ALU bit only): the ALU's lane dispatch takes an instruction's packets back to back, without the empty cycle between instructions (16 lanes, 32 threads: 3 cycles per instruction to 2). Calibrated toward the part: with 64 warps the load stream at 128 KB in flight goes from 76 to 106 GB/s (part 116; 103 at 64 KB against 96 here) and independent integer code from 1.29 to 1.90 instructions per cycle (part 3.58). KNOWN OVERSHOOT, accepted by the user on 2026-11-22, for large branch-dense loops only: with a branch in every instruction and the SM full the model runs at 1.59 / 1.94 instructions per cycle at 32 / 64 warps. Our H200 does 1.80-1.96 at 32 warps when the loop fits its instruction cache (1.6-3.2 KB of code) and 1.11 for a 12.4 KB loop (study/results_gpu/h200_brcap_summary.txt): the part's rate with two or more warps per processing block falls with code size, which fits a per-block instruction cache of limited capacity, and this model has no such effect (its test loop is 520 bytes against a 16 KB icache). So the model is within 3% of the part at 32 warps for a small loop and overshoots a 12 KB loop by 43%. The part's 64-warp figures come from two CTAs of 32 warps, of which the older takes the SM, so the 32-warp column is the reference. The study's workloads (GEMM, memory streams) are branch-sparse. The LSU bit (2) stays off until SimX's LSU input capacity fix lands. rtlsim and SimX agree with the bit set at small shapes (one warp within 0.1%; 16 warps x 32 threads 0.36%; 4 warps 0.95%, a lane-dispatch coupling difference in SimX still open). Not measured: logic depth
sources.BAR_DRAIN_SCOPE: 1: a stalling barrier waits for its own warp's instructions, and for the SM's requests still queued in the LSU or on their way to the data cache, any warp's and loads included, but not for the reads waiting at the caches and memory. CUDA's bar.sync orders a CTA's own accesses, and on a real H200 a barrier does not depend on other CTAs' loads: 16 CTAs per SM run 2503-2536 cycles per iteration whether they start in lockstep or staggered, and a barrier-only probe goes from 71 to 79 cycles beside streaming neighbours (study/results_gpu/h200_borrow_e4_*). With the core-wide drain a load-staged kernel had two rates (lockstep 15.8, staggered 14.7 GB/s per SM); with this it has one (22.2)
sources.TCU_FEDP2K, TCU_TMEM_ENABLE, TCU_TMEM_CO: Tensor core at the part's rate. An H100/H200 SM does 989.5 TFLOPS / 132 / 1.98 GHz = 3,786 FP16 FLOPs per clock; four blocks of 512 FMAs (FEDP2K) give a roof of 4,096. Hopper reaches it with wgmma tiles up to N = 256 held in up to 128 registers per thread; RISC-V has 32 FP registers, so the same tile width is held in tensor memory (Blackwell's structure) with 1,024 columns. With B fetched two blocks ahead and A read a bank row at a time the engine does 3,684 FLOPs per clock through the one 128 B/clock shared-memory port (1,787 as upstream; SimX and rtlsim agree within 1% at the CI and 32-thread shapes). wgmma is not available in a tensor-memory build. Not measured: logic depth and area of the fetch change
sources.LMEM_TCU_RDPORT: 1: the tensor core's shared-memory operand reads use the banks' read-only port instead of taking turns with the DXA's writes on one 128 B/clock port. Calibrated toward the part: an H200 SM takes 215-219 GB/s of TMA writes alone, 251-253 of shared-memory reads alone and 157-170 written then read, so writes and reads only partly share its shared-memory bandwidth, where one shared port capped a staged byte at 64 B/clock each way. Decode on one SM (gemm_tmem_decode -m16 -n8192 -k4096, KSTEPS=2 PIPE=6 XFER=8192): 82.0 GB/s of weights at 0, 100.3 at 1, then bound by the DXA's supply (write-only 116 at best); 4 SMs 66.9 to 70.7 per SM; 11 SMs unchanged (memory-bound). The tensor engine alone is unchanged to the cycle (tmem_roof 2391 / 3370 / 3704 FLOPs per clock at N = 128 / 256 / 512); gemm_tmem 3553 to 3762 in the multiply (part 3,786). The knob adds no read bytes to a clock: row reads and the LSU's read passes take the banks in turn, and at h200s (16 banks, 8 LSU lanes) reads total at most one 128 B row per clock; a DXA write and a row read of another row share a cycle. rtlsim and SimX agree within 1.6% on the tensor and DXA cases and 3.2% on tensor reads beside loads. The rule that bounds a row read's wait behind atomics or writes to its row has no failing test (it needs a bench on the local memory unit). Not measured: logic depth
sources.LMEM_WR_MERGE, LMEM_WR_ROW: 1: store lanes that write different bytes of one 8-byte bank word share its access, and each processing block's stores have their own pass engine, the banks bounding them at one row per clock. Calibrated toward the part: one H200 CTA stores 1.000 4-byte warp-instructions per clock at 8, 16 and 32 warps and one every 4.06 clocks with one warp (study/results_gpu/h200_smr_summary.txt). Here 0.083 per cycle before and 0.78 with both at 32 warps (-22%; 0.62 at 8 warps, -38%), one warp 12.4 cycles before and 5.6 after (+38%); the remainder is the LSU's packet gap and the lone-warp issue path. Loads are unchanged by these knobs (0.49 per cycle at 64 warps against the part's 1.000) and, while another block stores, make little progress (stores have priority; a turn rule is to follow), though in a mixed run both the storing and the loading warps finish sooner than with the knobs off (store warps 49,324 to 10,471 cycles per iteration, load warps 49,370 to 26,848). rtlsim and SimX agree within 0.16% on the store kinds at this lane shape. Not measured: logic depth
sources.DCACHE_FWD_HOLD: 1: a forwarded fill that finds the bank's 2-entry response queue full waits, as the RTL does (VX_cache_bank.sv fwd_head), instead of being replayed through the bank. Checked against rtlsim on one SM (bwstream -n64 -b32): rtlsim 20,570 cycles, SimX 20,266 with it and 25,824 without. With it 11 of the 22 SMs fill 91% of the memory peak with plain loads (a real H200 fills 90% with half its SMs)
sources.DCACHE_MSHR_SIZE, LSU_PENDING_LIMIT, LSU: 512 lines an SM may have outstanding. A real H200 SM streams 107 GB/s with plain loads (8 SMs under an MPS limit: 858 GB/s), which over the 659-cycle memory round trip is about 550 lines in flight. Measured on one SM, whole run, CUDA block shape (bwstream -b32 -u4): 512 lines give 51 GB/s, and 77 GB/s with DCACHE_FWD_HOLD. An earlier figure of 87 GB/s (and 109 with 16 dcache banks) came from differencing two run lengths of the one-stream-per-warp shape and was a measurement artifact; the bank count stays at the part's 4 (128 B per clock, h100) and the gap to 107 is open
